settings.prompt:
Autonomously review this Java source repository for potential security
vulnerabilities using the available read-only tools. Do not ask the user questions or summarize
tool output. Copy exact relative paths from list_files or index results; never invent or prefix a path.
A file listing or index hint is only navigation; inspect original source and seek
counter-evidence before deciding. Trace plausible untrusted input to security-sensitive
operations where possible, and check relevant guards and configuration. Report at most 10
candidates supported by exact source lines, with root cause, preconditions, counter-evidence,
and missing evidence. Do not assume a vulnerability exists. If source review finds no supported
candidate, submit an empty candidate list. Your final action must be submit_findings; natural
language commentary is not a report. Do not use project names, dataset identifiers, or a guessed
known answer as evidence.

counter_evidence: Deserialization is only reached when the route/component elects to treat the body as a serialized Java object; many routes never call these helpers (HttpHelper.java:239-266 are opt-in normalizers).

writeObjectToServletResponse's use of CONTENT_TYPE_JAVA_SERIALIZED_OBJECT shows the feature is a deliberate, symmetric serialization contract rather than accidental deserialization of arbitrary bodies.
No ObjectInputFilter usage was observed in the read source, so this is a design-pattern observation rather than a proven reachable vulnerability.
candidates.description: components/camel-http/src/main/java/org/apache/camel/component/http/helper/HttpHelper.java contains deserializeJavaObjectFromStream(ObjectInputStream) which directly delegates to the stream's readObject() and returns the resulting Object, with no ObjectInputFilter, class whitelist, or resolveClass override. The companion normalizeRequestToJavaObject / normalizeResponseToJavaObject methods (HttpHelper.java:239-266) invoke this helper, and writeObjectToServletResponse (HttpHelper.java:193-... / earlier span) sets HttpConstants.CONTENT_TYPE_JAVA_SERIALIZED_OBJECT, confirming that the component's Java-object exchange mode intentionally serializes and deserializes Java objects over HTTP. When a route (or a converter driven by the application/x-java-serialized-object content type) reaches this helper, the bytes are attacker-influenceable (peer/client/server response body), so native deserialization of those bytes could instantiate arbitrary classes/gadget chains present on the classpath. This is a pattern/design observation backed by the read source, not a demonstrated exploit: the class filtering is absent in the read methods, but reachability from a concrete untrusted-input route was not verified.
missing_evidence: Whether HttpConverter selects deserializeJavaObjectFromStream based on an attacker-controlled content type.
Whether any global JVM ObjectInputFilter, SecurityManager, or class-loading restriction is configured in deployments.
A concrete route plus request/response flow that reaches the helper with untrusted bytes.
preconditions: A Camel route uses camel-http in the Java-serialized-object exchange mode (content type application/x-java-serialized-object) or otherwise calls HttpHelper.normalizeRequestToJavaObject / normalizeResponseToJavaObject.
The attacker can influence the serialized byte stream returned to / handled by deserializeJavaObjectFromStream.
A usable gadget chain exists on the target classpath.
No JVM-wide or application-level ObjectInputFilter is configured.
candidates.title: Java native deserialization of untrusted bytes in camel-http HttpHelper
